title: Onboarding That Makes the Work and the Culture Understandable
audience: All staff supporting new colleagues; supervisor focus for onboarding design.

sources.title: One DSD: Naming team unwritten rules

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Onboarding That Makes the Work and the Culture Understandable
Examine how a usable welcome makes expectations, relationships, and support visible without requiring insider knowledge.
Intermediate self-directed learning
slides.narration: A new colleague can know the subject well and still need to learn how a particular team works. Onboarding should make that local knowledge available rather than turn the first assignment into a test of connections. This course considers service introductions and employee starts, with attention to sequence, unwritten rules, access, and useful feedback. You will examine the conditions people receive before judging their responses. No new timetable is prescribed; the focus is the quality of the route into the work.

slides.text:
The subject is familiar; the route is not
In this example, a new analyst understands the policy issue but cannot identify who reviews the first draft. The guide says they will pick it up.

Before interpreting the delay as poor judgment, ask what local information was actually available. Privately consider a question you once needed answered to begin unfamiliar work.
slides.narration: Experience in a field does not automatically supply knowledge of a team's review route. Staff who have used the process for years may no longer notice how much remains unstated. The newcomer may hesitate because they cannot tell who should receive the work or what ready means in this setting. That uncertainty deserves examination before a broad conclusion about competence. Your opening reflection stays with the task and the available explanation rather than requiring a personal story about belonging.

slides.text:
A welcome is an entry into meaningful work
Onboarding connects people with the purpose, expectations, relationships, resources, and support needed to contribute.

A completed checklist or a friendly greeting can help, but neither establishes that the work is understandable and usable. Examine what the arrangement actually makes possible.
slides.narration: A welcome has both human and practical dimensions. A colleague needs to feel respected and also to know how to start a real task. Information, access, and relationships work together: a name on a list helps more when the relevant role is explained. A checklist can confirm that something was sent without showing whether it was usable. The course treats onboarding as an experience to examine, rather than a ceremony that proves inclusion because every item has been checked.

slides.text:
A review route made visible
A newcomer misses an unstated draft-review step and receives feedback that they lack initiative. The same step is obvious to staff with established connections.

Explain the actual route and the expected result. Repeated hidden steps can influence early assignments and confidence; the mechanism needs evidence before becoming a finding.
slides.narration: The improved response makes the work clearer while preserving accountability. The employee still needs to prepare a useful draft and follow its actual review requirements. Staff should explain the relevant roles and give a shareable example where appropriate. The possible recurring barrier is that insider knowledge determines who can complete the first tasks smoothly. Compare what newcomers received and how concerns were handled before concluding that this process explains a pattern in feedback, development, or retention.

slides.text:
A service route unfamiliar to the person
A person knows the question they want answered but not the service's normal sequence. Which response is most useful?
A. Explain the actual next step and invite relevant clarification.
B. Assume they are not interested because they need orientation.
C. Give every policy document without identifying the next action.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: In this example, a service introduction assumes the person knows the normal sequence and familiar terms. The person arrives with a clear question but asks where the next step belongs. Consider the difference between knowing what they want explained and knowing an agency's local route. The response should preserve actual service conditions while making the next action usable. A repeated pattern of unexplained starts could affect who completes requests, but this encounter alone cannot establish that cause. Choose the response that examines the communication rather than assigning a personal deficit.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Explain the actual next step and invite relevant clarification.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Assume they are not interested because they need orientation.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Give every policy document without identifying the next action.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
A clear route supports the person's task while retaining real conditions. Ask what remains unclear.

What local knowledge does the explanation assume?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response makes the next action available without treating the person as incapable. Explain the actual contact or step and retain important service conditions. Ask what remains unclear and use appropriate support where needed. A clearer introduction may help this encounter, but later use and outcomes need their own evidence before a broader finding about access is made.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Unfamiliarity does not establish motivation. That inference could hide a repeated communication gap.

What local knowledge does the explanation assume?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A request for orientation tells you that local knowledge is missing, not that the person lacks interest. Describing them that way could influence later treatment and leave the confusing sequence unchanged. Examine what the service explanation made available and what the person was trying to do. Repeated gaps may form a barrier, but their actual effects require evidence.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
More material is not automatically usable. Connect the relevant information to the action.

What local knowledge does the explanation assume?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A large packet may contain relevant background while still leaving the next step hidden. The person needs an explanation connected to the question they brought. Organize the information around that task and preserve important conditions. More pages cannot establish understanding or successful action, so ask what the material communicates rather than assume volume supplies a usable introduction.

slides.text:
A sequence people can use
Separate what someone needs before beginning, what helps with the first task, and what becomes useful with more context.

Avoid delivering every resource as one undifferentiated packet. A usable sequence supports learning without assuming that one pace or format fits every person.
slides.narration: New information becomes easier to understand when it connects to a present purpose. A resource about a later process may be valuable but difficult to place before the person knows the basic task. Staff can organize the introduction around what is needed to begin, then explain further context as it becomes relevant. This course sets no schedule or prescribed duration. The question is whether the sequence helps the colleague find and use the information, with room for individual access needs and clarification.

slides.text:
Access that is ready for the task
Equipment, systems, materials, and meeting arrangements can determine whether someone can begin. A welcome email does not establish that those conditions work.

Use the appropriate access and support routes. Do not treat a preventable arrangement gap as proof that the colleague is unprepared.
slides.narration: A person may arrive ready to contribute while the necessary account, document format, or work arrangement is unavailable. That is an observable condition to examine. It does not tell staff whether the employee is capable or committed. Appropriate processes guide system access and individual accommodation needs; the course does not approve an arrangement. A useful start connects the task with the conditions needed to perform it and makes the source of assistance clear rather than leaving the newcomer to solve every gap privately.

slides.text:
The actual purpose of the first task
Explain the audience, intended result, review steps, and limits of an early assignment. An example should show why the work is useful.

Share material only through appropriate information rules. A practice exercise can support learning but must not be presented as an approved form or completed service decision.
slides.narration: An early assignment teaches more when the colleague can see what makes the result useful. A policy summary may need to separate evidence from a recommendation or preserve a service condition. Explain those features rather than ask for something ready to go without defining readiness. Appropriate examples can help, provided they are shareable and their status is clear. The work still requires judgment, but the employee should know which judgment the task calls for and where clarification belongs.

slides.text:
Habit, agreement, and actual authority
A team habit is not automatically a required process. Ask where an expectation comes from and what it accomplishes.

Explain genuine requirements accurately. Unwritten preferences should not be presented as agency authority merely because experienced staff follow them.
slides.narration: A newcomer may encounter instructions about how drafts look, when people speak, or whom they approach first. Some have a real process basis; others are habits shaped over time. Distinguishing them helps the employee understand what must be retained and what can be discussed. This is not an invitation to ignore requirements. It is a request to verify their source and explain their purpose. Repeatedly turning preferences into rules can narrow participation while making the resulting difficulty appear to be the person's fault.

slides.text:
A new colleague and an informal decision channel
The team settles draft questions in a conversation the new employee does not know exists. The colleague is later judged for missing the outcome.

Make the relevant information and route visible. Examine the expectation before interpreting a different starting point as weak initiative or poor fit.
slides.narration: Informal conversations can help experienced staff coordinate, but important work information should not depend entirely on discovering them by chance. The newcomer may have followed every stated instruction and still missed an unstated decision. The appropriate response examines what was available and how the relevant outcome can be made visible. If this pattern recurs, it can influence early feedback and access to meaningful assignments. Do not infer the full effect from one event; use it to identify a question for actual process review.

slides.text:
An analyst misses an informal review
A new analyst misses a review step known only through informal conversation. What should be examined before a broad performance judgment?
A. Whether the analyst socializes like established staff.
B. What expectations and review information were actually available.
C. Whether the analyst can guess the route on a second attempt.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: In this example, a new DSD analyst prepares a first draft but misses a review step. Established staff know about that step through informal conversations; the guide never names it. The analyst has relevant subject knowledge and asks for clarification. Consider which evidence should be examined before a broad judgment about performance or initiative. The strongest response does not remove the need for good work. It makes the local expectation understandable and keeps feedback connected to the actual draft, available information, and support.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Whether the analyst socializes like established staff.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. What expectations and review information were actually available.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Whether the analyst can guess the route on a second attempt.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A social style is not automatically evidence of the work capability. The missing route needs attention.

Was the expectation understandable before it was used to judge the work?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Some social relationships help colleagues learn, but a preferred social style should not become the only route to essential work information. The analyst's missed review may reflect the hidden process rather than lack of commitment. Make the actual route visible and examine the work evidence. Repeated dependence on informal connections can affect early assignments and development opportunity.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Compare the stated task, local information, support, and actual work. Then give specific guidance and feedback.

Was the expectation understandable before it was used to judge the work?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response separates an orientation gap from the quality of the draft. The analyst may need both a clear review route and specific feedback on the work. Explain the actual expectation and examine whether other newcomers faced the same missing information. The course does not decide a real performance issue; it prepares a more supportable question about evidence and conditions.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Guessing repeats the original gap. Make the real expectation visible rather than turn orientation into a test.

Was the expectation understandable before it was used to judge the work?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Another attempt without explanation leaves the colleague to reconstruct the same route. A fortunate guess would not prove that the introduction is sound, and another miss would not automatically establish poor judgment. Name the actual review step and its purpose. Accountability can remain while staff improve the information the employee needs to carry out the task.

slides.text:
Relationships with an explained purpose
An introduction should explain how the person or role helps with the work. A list of names leaves the newcomer to infer the relationship.

Offer useful connections without making belonging a performance. People need not socialize in the same way to contribute and cooperate professionally.
slides.narration: Some colleagues build relationships through informal conversation; others prefer a clear work reason for making contact. An introduction can support both by explaining what the role contributes and how a question might be raised. Avoid interpreting quietness or a different social preference as a lack of commitment. The goal is meaningful access to cooperation, not a required style of sociability. Examine whether the relationship route helps the employee obtain information and contribute, rather than measure success by comfort in one familiar setting.

slides.text:
Support without an identity assignment
A buddy can help locate routine information, if the purpose is clear. The arrangement does not replace task direction or formal support roles.

Do not choose someone simply to explain a shared identity or community. Ask about actual expertise, willingness, and workload through the relevant process.
slides.narration: An experienced colleague can make local information easier to find. That helpful role needs a boundary so it does not become unlimited support work or an identity-based duty. A person may share a background with the newcomer without being the right source for every question. The supervisor and designated offices retain their actual responsibilities. Culture briefs and shared learning can deepen understanding of communities served without requiring either employee to teach a whole group's experience. A useful connection recognizes expertise and choice.

slides.text:
Feedback that supports the next attempt
Name the expected result, what the work shows, and what could improve. Explain the missing local context where it matters.

Feedback should not turn a question into a character judgment. An employee can need orientation and still be accountable for applying the guidance they receive.
slides.narration: Specific feedback makes learning possible. If a draft does not distinguish a requirement from an option, explain that feature and show what the audience needs. If the review route was never explained, acknowledge the orientation gap rather than simply label the employee careless. The two concerns can coexist: staff can improve the introduction and still provide useful feedback on the work. Repeated vague judgments may shape development opportunities, so make the connection between the evidence and the improvement understandable.

slides.text:
Community knowledge as shared learning
Briefs can help a team prepare questions about services and communities. They cannot prescribe a new colleague's interests or representative role.

Invite relevant expertise and individual perspectives. Learning about people served belongs in shared professional development, not only on employees assumed to know a community by identity.
slides.narration: A new employee may bring experience that enriches service learning, but the team should not decide what they must teach from their identity. Use reviewed resources and appropriate community relationships to prepare and deepen questions. An individual can contribute voluntarily within their actual expertise and interests. Differences within communities remain important. This approach keeps the newcomer focused on meaningful work and chosen development while making community-informed practice a responsibility that the whole team can learn about.

slides.text:
The service introduction has a similar question
A person entering a service is told to follow the normal sequence but does not know its terms or contacts.

Explain the route and the next choice in usable language. Do not treat unfamiliarity with the system as evidence of lack of interest or ability.
slides.narration: A service start differs from employment, but both can depend on local knowledge that experienced staff take for granted. Someone may know what they need and still not understand the agency's sequence or vocabulary. Staff should explain the actual route, preserve service conditions, and invite relevant questions. A culture brief can help prepare communication considerations while individual preferences guide support. The evidence should describe what the person could understand and do, rather than infer motivation from an unfamiliar first encounter.

slides.text:
A community teaching role assigned by identity
A newcomer is assigned to teach a community overview because of their identity. Their stated interest is legislative research. What is the better approach?
A. Require the overview as proof of belonging.
B. Stop all community learning for the team.
C. Ask about actual expertise and chosen interests; use appropriate shared resources.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: In this example, a newcomer tells the supervisor they want to deepen legislative research skills. The team instead asks them to teach an overview of a community because of their identity. Community learning is valuable, and the colleague may have relevant knowledge, but neither fact establishes a representative duty. Consider how a welcome can recognize individual expertise without replacing the employee's stated direction. Repeated assignments could affect development and workload. Choose the response that preserves shared learning while asking about the colleague's actual interests and contribution.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Require the overview as proof of belonging.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Stop all community learning for the team.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Ask about actual expertise and chosen interests; use appropriate shared resources.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Belonging should not depend on representing a whole community. The assignment may displace chosen development.

Is the colleague's own professional direction being heard?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: An employee's identity does not establish a representative duty or make explanatory work a test of belonging. They may choose to share knowledge, but the team should ask about actual expertise and interests. Repeated assignments of this kind could affect workload and access to legislative development. Examine that possibility without assuming every such invitation has the same effect.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Community learning remains important. The concern is an assumed individual duty.

Is the colleague's own professional direction being heard?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Ending all community learning would discard a useful part of professional development. The better response distinguishes shared learning from a duty assigned through identity. Reviewed briefs can prepare questions, and appropriate partners or willing experts can contribute. The newcomer should have room for their own professional interests rather than be made the sole source of knowledge about a community.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Recognize expertise and choice. Briefs and appropriate relationships can support shared learning without identity-based expectations.

Is the colleague's own professional direction being heard?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response makes the colleague's expertise and chosen development visible. It does not prevent a voluntary contribution to community learning. Appropriate resources and relationships can support the whole team's understanding, while the employee focuses on meaningful work and interests. A respectful welcome should not require one person to carry an unlimited representative or explanatory role.

slides.text:
The effect of repeated unequal starts
Hidden information, unavailable support, and informal connections can interact across onboarding and early development.

Trace the arrangement, the response, and the later opportunity. Unequal starting conditions may contribute to differences, but a finding needs evidence and alternative explanations.
slides.narration: The systemic inquiry connects an initial gap with what follows. A newcomer who cannot find a review route may miss early work, receive vague feedback, and be offered fewer development tasks. That is a plausible sequence, not a conclusion established by the example. Examine each link and consider genuine task differences or other conditions. A revised start should be assessed for what it enables. Completion of an onboarding checklist is useful evidence about the checklist, but not automatically about later opportunity or retention.

slides.text:
Review the experience, not gratitude
Ask which instructions helped, where the person had to guess, and what support remained difficult to obtain.

A positive welcome response does not establish that the work was usable. Keep private information protected and distinguish process questions from performance evidence.
slides.narration: People may appreciate colleagues while still finding the arrangement confusing. Questions about gratitude or sociability can hide that distinction. A concrete review asks how the person began a task and where they needed unavailable information. Their account can identify a gap without becoming the whole explanation of later performance. Appropriate records and task evidence can add context. Keep the purpose and privacy clear, and do not require disclosure of personal experiences to justify a suggestion about the onboarding route.

slides.text:
Rewrite an unwritten instruction
Privately revise: 'You will learn who needs to see the draft as you go.'

Use a review route. Explain the relevant role, expected result, and source of clarification. Mark any real process detail that would need confirmation instead of inventing it.
slides.narration: The revision should make an important expectation available before the colleague is judged against it. In a practice example, you can identify who reviews the draft and why, along with what the writer should bring to the review. A real instruction needs confirmation through the actual process. Then ask whether the revision would help someone without existing connections begin the work. This is a private examination of clarity, not a request to disclose a colleague's difficult start or personal circumstances.

slides.text:
Carry understanding through transitions
A new assignment, supervisor, system, or team can create another unfamiliar start. Do not assume earlier orientation covers every change.

Keep necessary information and appropriate support connected to the changed work. Development and advancement should not become occasions for silently losing useful conditions.
slides.narration: Onboarding reasoning remains relevant later in the employee life cycle. An experienced person may enter a different policy area or begin using a new system. Their subject knowledge does not remove the need for a clear route into that work. Examine what changed and what support should continue through the appropriate process. A transition can offer growth without being an unexamined test of working without information. The useful account distinguishes the new task, the arrangement, and what the evidence actually shows.

slides.text:
A welcome that makes contribution possible
Make expectations, relationships, access, and support understandable. Connect feedback to the actual work and the conditions available.

Examine repeated gaps without treating a different start as a personal deficit. A useful introduction respects the colleague and makes room for substantive contribution.
slides.narration: The strongest welcome combines warmth with a practical route into the work. It explains what matters, helps people find the relevant relationships, and offers a usable way to clarify uncertainty. It does not require newcomers to prove belonging through a familiar social style or discover essential information by chance. Continue examining whether the arrangement supports contribution across onboarding and transitions. That approach preserves accountability while recognizing the difference between a person's capability and the local conditions they were given.

outcomes: Explain work expectations and unwritten norms without making newcomers guess.
Make information, access support, and relationships usable from the start.
Avoid assigning cultural education or representation to a new colleague.
Connect early feedback with actual work evidence and opportunities to learn.
